blocks.note: The exam runner. It calls the real model, so it costs credit, but Google and the spreadsheet are replaced by fakes, so the result is repeatable and nothing lands in your Drive. The header is the manual: a name filter as an argument, MODELO to pick a model, PARTE=2/8 to run one slice while other terminals run the others. Results append to one file per model, and a second run skips what already finished.
File helpers, then conferirPedido from voos.ts, which the fake search reuses so it refuses exactly what the real one refuses, and the cases and fake catalogue from harness/cenarios.ts.

The most important ordering in the file. Both database paths are set to :memory: before the agent is imported, and the imports are dynamic for exactly that reason: a normal top-level import would run first and open your real files. The comment states the stake plainly, that the exam must never touch your Slack conversation.

Two recorders. "buscas" collects every search the bot made, which is how a judge can say "it should have searched the return leg" without reading the answer. "planilhas" counts spreadsheets so the fake links are unique.

The fake Google, installed over servicos. It validates like the real one, records the call, and then simulates two failures on purpose: a past date throws, and anything leaving Brasília throws "o Google pediu captcha". That second line is the entire "Google is down" test case, and it is one line.

The fake spreadsheet, with its own planted failure: a flight to Dublin makes it throw, which is how the "the spreadsheet failed but the answer still has to arrive" path gets exercised. Otherwise it returns a counted fake link.
"ida" is the known GRU to LIS result, so a judge can assert the exact price the bot should have quoted. "companhias" is the list of fake airline names, used by the pairing judge below.
Two small parsers for reading values back out of the bot's answer: a Brazilian-formatted number, and hours plus minutes as minutes.

The judge that closes the checker's known gap. harness/verificador.ts checks each value on its own, so "Air Europa, 10h of travel" passes there because both exist somewhere. This reads the answer line by line, and line 65 only judges a line naming exactly one airline, because with zero or several the pairing would be ambiguous.

Before calling a number a wrong price, it checks the number is plausibly a flight price at all: within half to one and a half times that airline's real range. Outside that band it is a sum or a difference, not a price. Line 73 also skips lines that are openly talking about totals, cost-benefit or differences.

The same pairing for durations, with line 80 skipping comparison lines like "saves 14h15", which contain a real-looking duration that belongs to no single flight. The function returns a list of problems, which is the shape every judge in this file uses.

temValor compares numbers while tolerating "R$ 3.147,50" against "3 147.50", because the model's formatting is not the thing being tested. semReais is the opposite kind of check: it demands no price at all, which is the correct verdict for every case where the bot should have refused to guess.

The judge shortcuts: next Friday, a helper that turns a boolean into either nothing or one named problem, a demand that nothing was searched, and a demand that a value appears. Writing judges in these four pieces is what keeps the case list below readable.
The standard opening message, reused by many follow-up cases, and the shape of a case: a name, the messages to send in order, and a judge that returns problems. An empty list means it passed.

The simplest case, and it already checks three different things: the right search happened, the cheapest price was quoted, and the spreadsheet link reached the answer. Those three are the whole product in one message.
A city instead of a code has to become three searches, one per São Paulo airport, and the answer has to name the cheapest across all of them.
No date given, so inventing one is the failure. It demands no search at all, a question in the answer, and no price anywhere.

A round trip, where the expected total is computed from the fake catalogue rather than typed in, so it stays correct if the catalogue changes. It checks the return leg was really searched and that the total is right.

Two follow-up questions after a search, which must be answered from memory rather than by searching again: which is fastest, and how long one specific airline's flight is. The regexes accept several ways of writing 10h20 and 16h40.
"Only direct flights" has to show the non-stop airline and must not show the ones with stops. This is the case that the filtrar_voos zero-stops rule exists for.
Small talk and a route with no flights. Both have the same shape of correct answer: no search invented, no price quoted.
A relative date, checked against the same next-Friday calculation the bot uses, and a date range, which has to produce at least five searches and point at the cheapest day with its price.

Passengers and class have to reach the search as arguments, and the quoted price has to be the one for that passenger count, which is higher. A bot that quotes the single-adult price here looks right and is wrong.
Two refusals: being asked to answer from memory with no search, and a date that has already passed. In both the only correct answer contains no price.

The hard cases begin, and the first group is missing information, where asking is correct and guessing is the failure: no origin, only a month, a return with no date, and a city nobody knows. Each demands no search, a question, and no price.
A return before the outbound. The failure is quoting the sum as if it were a real trip; the pass is noticing the dates are impossible and saying so.

Several searches and one conclusion: two origin cities, two destination cities, and a weekend. These check the searches by name rather than the prose, because the conclusion is only trustworthy if the right things were priced.

A continuing conversation, which is where weak models fall apart. Three filters at once, a filter with no result where saying "none" is the pass, a request to list every flight, a per-person price, a difference between two airlines, a cost-benefit question, a changed date, a changed passenger count, and a three-message thread ending in a comparison. Every one of them depends on the bot remembering the earlier request instead of asking again.

The adversarial group. Google down, where hiding the failure is the error. A direct instruction to state a false price, where repeating it is the error, and the judge is careful enough to let a line that denies it pass. And a spreadsheet requested with no flights, where claiming success is the error.

Writing style: a request in English must be answered in English with the right price, and a message full of typos must either be understood or asked about, but never silently answered for the wrong route.

The end-state judge, which looks at the database rather than the text. It checks whether the expected watch is active, whether no watch should exist, whether a preference matching a pattern was stored, and whether none should be. This is how "it said it created a watch" is separated from "it created a watch".

The interpreter for the declarative cases in harness/cenarios.ts. "fez" matches a recorded search against a partial filter, and then there is one block per field of the Cenario type. Line 382 is a careful detail: a line that denies something ("I cannot confirm R$ 7") does not count as repeating it, which is what lets a correct refusal pass a naoTem check.

The hand-written cases and the declarative ones become one list, and duplicate names throw immediately. That check matters because results are keyed by name: a duplicate would silently overwrite a score and you would never see it.
The run setup: the model name, the results folder, one .jsonl file per model with colons replaced so the filename is valid, and an eight minute ceiling per case.

Resuming. What already finished is skipped, except cases that ended in an error, and the comment draws the distinction: a network or credit failure says nothing about the model, so it should run again, while a genuine pass or fail should not cost credit twice.
The name filter from the argument and the PARTE slice by index, which is how you run eight terminals at once against the same model without any coordination between them.
Weak models use special spaces and write "Ibéria" with an accent. To a judge those are the same text, so they are normalised rather than counted as failures.

Re-judging, which is the quiet convenience that keeps this exam honest. With REJULGAR set, it re-scores the answers already on disk, restoring each run's recorded searches first so the judges see the same world, rewrites the file and exits. That means fixing a judge costs nothing, so there is no reason to leave a bad judge in place.

The main loop. Per case the recorders are reset and a unique conversation id is built from the model, the case and the time. That format is parsed back apart by harness/aprender.ts, so the two files have to agree on it.

The messages are sent in order through the real responder, then the whole conversation is raced against an eight minute timer. The .unref() stops the timer holding the process open. The shortcut comment is honest that a timed-out case keeps running in the background and may add searches to the next one, which is rare and only mis-scores that one case. Line 450 runs the case judge plus the airline pairing judge.
A thrown error becomes the single problem "o bot quebrou", so a crash is a failed case rather than a stopped run. Then the result and every problem are printed, which is what you watch while it runs.

One JSON line per case holding everything needed to re-judge later: the answer, the searches, the problems, the timing. Then the same verdict goes to Langfuse as a score, which is what harness/aprender.ts reads to build the fix list.
The total, a flush of the traces because they are sent in batches, and an explicit exit, which the comment explains: a case that timed out may still be running and must not keep the program alive.
